newsitem.title: UK: London PGM tensions ease, prices hold gains.
newsitem.headline: London PGM tensions ease, prices hold gains.

text.p: Recent tensions in platinum and palladium (PGM) prices abated on Wednesday encouraging some two-way business and dealers to more freely offer to lend metal for forward dates.
Extreme tightness of material has squeezed the market since major exporter Russia suspended shipments due to administrative and political changes last December.
"The panic seemed to haved peaked last week," one dealer said of the platinum and palladium markets.

Prices raced to seven-year highs for platinum and 17 year peaks for palladium last week and dealers suspended quoting borrowing rates for the metals after the rate for one month palladium soared to around 300 percent.
"Dealers have made a conscious effort to keep a responsible market and to keep the market trading," one dealer said.
Dealers began quoting forward rates again at around 100 percent for a month for platinum and 120 percent for palladium.

Indicating the shortage of material was concentrated on the "nearby" dates, the borrowing cost of three-months platinum and palladium was only 60 percent and 80 percent respectively, still enormous compared with the more regular two-four percent.
Reports from Japanese trade houses in Tokyo quoting Russian export negotiators in the city indicating spot market sales of the metals could begin late June have eased market tensions.
The Russian export agency Almaz has been granted export licences and first 1997 deliveries to Japan are forecast for July 10, according to Japanese traders.
"These issues are factored in to the price," a dealer said.

One of the reasons palladium rose overnight was the change of tactics on Tokyo's Tocom futures market which saw speculators closing out positions which anticipated prices falling further as Russian exports began.
Gold fixed just 10 cents firmer than its morning setting at $343.80 per ounce. The August gold contract on Comex was unchanged at $346.10.
Dealers said the perception that gold's upside was tightly limited and with the summer season trading lull settling over the market, that was unlikely to change near term.
"It has to break through $345.00 to get back on to an uptrend," one dealer said.
